Issued at 1228 PM CDT Tue Oct 6 2026

Quiet weather looks to be in store through the remainder of the
work week and into the first half of the weekend. A bit more
unsettled and uncertain for the latter half of the weekend and
into next week. 

Currently, high pressure was building southeast over the area
behind a weak dry cold front. Winds were generally 10 to 15 mph
with a few gusts in the 20 to 25 mph range. Humidities were
mainly 20 to 25% over southwest and far south central ND this 
afternoon, with a few readings under 20% in Bowman county. Winds
are expected remain in this range or just a bit stronger for a 
few more hours, then drop off pretty quickly late this afternoon
into early evening. Will maintain near critical fire weather 
conditions in the far southwest. 

For tonight, we did utilize a blend of NBM and NBM10 to get some
lower temperatures in the forecast, which seems reasonable 
given clear to partly cloudy skies and light winds. This has 
been the case the last couple of nights. A sprinkle or isolated 
shower can not be ruled out in the north central as upper level 
jet energy swings through here tonight. 

Wednesday and Thursday will be a little cooler than today with
highs mainly in the lower 60s to lower 70s. Lows Thursday
morning are forecast to be in the mid 30s to mid 40s. 

Upper level ridging takes place over the northern Plains Friday
and into the weekend ahead of a digging western trough. There
has been a lot of uncertainty in the evolution of this system
and the uncertainty still remains. However, here's a few things
we do know. 

As the upper low drop south into the Pacific Northwest Friday 
night into Saturday, there is good agreement that energy with 
this system splits. A portion of the energy will continue to 
drop south with a possible closed upper low around the West 
Coast. A portion of the energy will also propagate eastward 
along the International Border as a northern stream wave. This 
would put better precipitation chances northeast and southwest 
of the forecast area. There will be a cold front that drops 
through our area, and in looking at the NBM Viewer, the 
probability of a tenth of an inch or more of liquid from 12Z 
Sunday through 12Z Monday ranges from 20-30 percent in the James
River Valley to 60-70 percent over southwest ND (and 30 to 50% 
northwest and central ND). The initial precipitation chances 
look to be delayed a bit, and there's a lot of uncertainty in 
how far the cold front drop through the area, and this will have
implications on where the more vigorous forcing will set up. 
The cold front does continue to sag southward early next week, 
so low to medium precipitation chances may linger over the area 
into Tuesday, bringing additional chance for generally light qpf
amounts. 

It will be significantly colder by late weekend and early next 
week, especially given our recent spell of above normal
temperatures. However, the magnitude of the cold air remains in
question. Latest deterministic and ensemble model runs are 
backing off a bit on how cold it gets Sunday and Monday.
Currently, highs on Sunday range form the mid 40s northwest to
the mid 60s in the southern James River Valley. On Monday, highs
are currently forecast to range from the mid 40s to lower 50s,
with upper 40s to mid 50s forecast for Tuesday. With the colder
temperatures, we could see a little mix of rain and snow Sunday
night into Monday morning, and again Monday night into Tuesday
morning. Any snow amounts look to be negligible at this time.

From a cluster analysis standpoint, the consensus is that the
upper level energy that drops south Friday night into Saturday
will close off over the western U.S. A cluster analysis centered
on the Monday evening through Tuesday evening timeframe shows
practically a 70 percent probability for a closed upper low over
the Great Basin area, with upper ridging to it's north and east,
including over North Dakota. This is compared to a 30 percent
probability for a more progressive trough tracking through the
northern Plains. Of the 70 percent probability, remarkably, there
is quite an equal weighting of the 3 separate model cores. The 
question then becomes, what happens if/when this closed upper 
low lifts back into our neck of the woods. Well, that's beyond 
the end of our forecast so you'll have to tune back at a later 
date to find out.
